failure_modes.description: The assumption that simple local rules can produce complex global optimization is fundamentally flawed without considering network-wide coordination effects
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic networks exhibit non-linear dynamics where local optimizations often create global bottlenecks (Braess paradox)

failure_modes.description: Direct contradicts established traffic flow theory which shows that optimal signal coordination requires explicit timing plans
failure_modes.evidence: All major metropolitan areas use coordinated signal timing systems with fixed offsets, not purely local rules

failure_modes.description: Fails to account for boundary conditions like network entry/exit points and major arterials that cannot be controlled by local rules alone
failure_modes.evidence: Network boundaries create fundamental asymmetries that prevent true self-organization

failure_modes.description: Numerous existing adaptive signal systems use more sophisticated approaches than simple threshold rules
failure_modes.evidence: SCATS, SCOOT, and RHODES systems all use predictive algorithms and network-wide coordination

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis predicts emergence of optimal patterns, but real-world implementations show exactly the oscillations and instabilities predicted as failure modes
failure_modes.evidence: Multiple studies show simple local rules create 'traffic waves' that propagate through networks, worsening congestion

failure_modes.description: The target of 'system-level optimization' is mathematically ill-defined without specifying optimization criteria
failure_modes.evidence: Different optimization goals (throughput vs. delay vs. emissions) lead to conflicting signal timing requirements
